blocks.text: So first of all, I got voted to do the presentation because I talk faster and can condense it down. We did a rate study in 2022 and normally we do rate studies for five years. and we based that race study on what we projected as industrial flows, what we had been led to believe. In that study, we adjusted rates among the various classes, we adjusted the capacity fees, and we recommended rate increases for 23, 24, 25, 26, and 27, and those were adopted, wastewater rates were adopted by council, water rates were adapted by the service safety director. In the meantime, industrial flows did not increase as much as predicted, so we got a little nervous. Project cost increased due to all those things the mayor's talked about. Inflation, labor costs, supply chain, time delays. We also had additional EPA regulations, including lead copper, asset management, risk assessment, and increased sampling requirements. And this is kind of never ending. We were in a call this morning with Ohio EPA, and they want to reopen the long-term control plan and look at what the next phase on that might be. So looking at all of those things, as I said, we got nervous in water and water pollution, decided that maybe we needed to go in and take a look at this midterm. so we didn't get a surprise at the very end and we could make gradual rate adjustments. I did send you the redacted rate study. It was redacted in accordance with the Ohio Revised Code. If you've got questions on something that was redacted, let us know and we can talk you through that. What we predicted would work at 3%, 3% for 26 and 27, we extended it two more years because we're two more years into a five-year rate study. So that projected out. So that worked out fine. On the water side, what we found was, Even with the recommended rate adjustments, we were going to be short. And a lot of that was due to the fact that the division of water was requesting $2 million for asset management, preventative maintenance projects. We are just so behind on things. We went for years without rate increases. We went for years saying, if we can just get the South water plant paid off, we can put money into the system. and when we paid off the south water plant we started on the north water plant so division water has a huge backlog they requested two million dollars a year so this would be what it would look like then we talked about the philosophy of water charges and there's basically three philosophies they're all valid depending on what you want to do the first philosophy is what we currently have which is a declining rate under declining rate system a larger portion of the cost is pushed down on the lower water users and we the larger water users get a break on each hundred cubic feet of water that they use in a declining water rate you it's done to encourage big water users to locate well guess what we got our big water user flat rate communities are communities that basically their philosophy is a gallon of water is a gallon of water and it doesn't matter if it's going to your house or if it's going to the hospital or if it's going to an industrial user a gallon of water cost what a gallon water cost then there are a few communities that have increasing rates. These communities tend to want to conserve their water capacity so they tend to want to have smaller users or encourage water conservation. So we looked at us being a declining rate community and said well what if we go to a flat rate? We've been a declining rate community for about 10 years. So if If we would go to and phase out our declining rates, this is what the rates would look like. And as you can see in 26, we're starting to bump up those higher water users.
